ABSTRACT

INTEGRATING INDIGENOUS CONSERVATION PRACTICES INTO WETLAND MANAGEMENT POLICIES: A CASE STUDY OF NIGER DELTA AND WEST AFRICA REGION

Journal: Environment & Ecosystem Science (EES)

Author: Isikong, S. S, Ansa, I. E, Aniefiok, I. S. and Davies I. O.

This is an open access article distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution License CC BY 4.0, which permits unrestricted use, distribution, and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited

DOI: 10.26480/ees.02.2026.131.137

Wetlands constitute some of the world most productive and ecologically significant ecosystems, providing essential services such as biodiversity conservation, flood control and regulation, carbon sequestration, and livelihood support. Inspite of their importance, wetlands ecosystem across West Africa, particularly in the Niger Delta of Nigeria, are experiencing accelerated degradation due to human exploitation, rapid urbanization, climate change, and weak governance structures. Contemporary wetlands management policies in the region are largely dominated by centralized, top-bottom regulatory approaches that often overlook indigenous conservation practices and local ecological knowledge system. This paper examines the integration of indigenous conservation practices into wetlands ecosystem management policies, using the Niger Delta region of Nigeria, with specific reference to Akwa Ibom State, as a case study. Adopting a mixedmethods research design, the study draws on household surveys, key informant interviews, focus group discussions, field observations, and policy document analysis to examine the nature, effectiveness, and institutional relevance of indigenous conservation practices in wetland-dependent communities. The findings reveal that practices such as sacred wetland protection, fishing taboos, seasonal harvesting restrictions, customary land-use regulations, and communal enforcement mechanisms play a critical role in regulating resource use, conserving biodiversity, and strengthening community stewardship. However, these practices remain inadequately recognized and poorly integrated into formal wetlands management frameworks, resulting in limited community participation, weak compliance, and persistent ecological degradation. The study concludes that indigenous knowledge conservation practices represent adaptive and culturally legitimate governance systems capable of complementing statutory wetlands management policies. It recommends that the institutional integration of indigenous knowledge systems through participatory policy design, legal recognition of customary institutions, and co-management arrangements. By bridging indigenous and formal governance systems, the study contributes to advancing inclusive, resilient, and sustainable wetlands management in the Niger Delta Region of Nigeria and the wider West
African region.
